newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Krupp-rate rise now would be very damaging.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Krupp-rate rise now would be very damaging.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Krupp said on Monday the recent sharp weakening of the mark was worrying but that a German interest rate rise now would be severely damaging to the domestic economy.

Krupp said in the text of a speech that a small interest rate rise would probably have little impact on exchange rates while a larger increase would not be justifiable given continued weakness in the domestic economy.
"...there is pressure on the central bank to raise interest rates for currency reasons," Krupp said. "But an interest rate increase would be highly damaging for domestic economic reasons."

Krupp said the mark's appreciation of 1995 had been reversed and that exchange rates now more closely matched the currencies' respective purchasing power. "But the current situation is also creating problems", he said.

He noted that the mark's external value had fallen about six percent in the first seven months of 1997 and said the speed of the decline was worrying. Nevertheless, he saw no inflationary dangers resulting from the mark's fall.
"Such a depreciation can lead to imported inflation. The continued weak economy means that no inflation movement is discernible at the moment," Krupp said.

A text of the speech, to be held at a conference on European monetary union, was made available ahead of delivery. Krupp is president of the state central bank of Hamburg, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Schleswig-Holstein.
Krupp said the most recent slight rise in German inflation was caused by changes to the health care system and car taxation.
"The rise in import prices has significantly flattened out," Krupp said, noting that the annual rise over the last six months was just 1.5 percent.

German consumer inflation rose to a year-on-year rate of 1.9 percent in July from 1.7 percent in June, with the month-on-month rate rising to 0.5 percent from 0.2 percent following a rise in prescription charges and the introduction of new tax rates for car owners in July.

Krupp said that overall, exchange rate turbulence had the effect of weakening economic growth because it weakened domestic demand in countries with appreciating currencies and caused inflationary pressure and interest rate rises where currencies were depreciating.

"Nation states have limited scope to react to exchange rate swings," Krupp said. National central banks did not have sufficient tools to prevent their currencies from being hit by currency turbulence.

Small countries in particular had limited capabilities to cope with swings but even large nations like Japan were not in a position to achieve exchange rates which did not diminish output and trade, Krupp said.
Of all tools, interest rate changes may have the most chance of success, he said.

The Bundesbank had been very reticent on this issue in the past but in its July 24 statement on its M3 money supply target it had not ruled out an exchange rate-oriented interest rate strategy, Krupp said.
"But that does not answer the question of how large the interest rate change should be to influence the exchange rate.

"There is much to suggest that a small interest rate rise would have no significant impact on the exchange rate, and a bigger interest rate rise, whose impact would also be uncertain, could not be justified in domestic economic terms.
"At the present Germany is a very good example of the dilemma of central banks."
With nations unable to solve the problems of a globalised economy, international cooperation was necessary and European monetary union was probably the only chance to improve conditions, Krupp said.

"Currency turbulence can no longer have an effect where no exchange rates exist. In addition, the size of the euro block means that swings of the dollar and the yen against the euro should be smaller than today against the mark."
--David Crossland, Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525
